text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.75. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.75.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.75 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 45 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
Working through the payoff structure: each token kept privately gives 1 point to self but costs the other three members 0.75 each, a net group loss, while each token put into the group account gives 0.75 back to the contributor with no negative externality on others.

Individually, keeping is the dominant strategy since 1 exceeds 0.75, but collectively full contribution does much better than full defection — this is the classic public goods dilemma. Given it's a repeated 10-round game, I'm leaning toward starting with a meaningfully cooperative contribution to try to signal and establish trust, rather than purely maximizing my own short-term payoff.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through the payoff structure: each member keeps some tokens privately (earning 1 point each but imposing a 0.75 externality cost on each of the other three members) versus contributing to the group account (earning 0.75 points to the contributor with no externality). I'm setting up the math to figure out my own points based on how many tokens I keep versus contribute.

Re-reading the rules, only the contributor gets the 0.75 payoff from group tokens, so there's no sharing through G after all. This makes private tokens individually dominant (1 vs 0.75, with no personal cost to me from the externality), even though socially the group token is better since keeping private costs others 2.25 total for my gain of just 1.

Since this is a repeated 10-round game, full cooperation yields each player 60 points versus 20 points if everyone keeps everything private. Given the clear mutual benefit, I'll start by contributing all 20 tokens to the group account to signal cooperation, even though there's risk of being exploited by free-riders.

Though defecting is individually dominant, the framing emphasizes group welfare, so I decide the sensible move is to contribute all 20 tokens to the group each round.

I'm working through the public goods game payoffs: keeping a token yields 1 point to the owner but costs each of the other three members 0.75, while contributing it to the group yields 0.75 to the contributor with no direct cost to others. If everyone contributes all 20 tokens, the group pool hits 80, multiplied by 0.75 to find each member's share.

Since individually keeping a token (1 point) beats contributing it (0.75 point) in private terms, the dominant strategy is to defect even though full cooperation maximizes collective welfare — classic free-rider tension. For round 1, though, I think signaling cooperation makes sense, so I'll contribute all 20 tokens to the group account as a starting move, possibly shifting strategy based on how others behave in later rounds.

The group total is 80: I gave 20, so the other three contributed 60 combined, meaning each of them also gave their full 20. That checks out with my payoff of 60 (45 base plus 15 from my contribution), confirming everyone cooperated fully.

I'll keep cooperating and contribute 20 again.

That's the classic rational defection logic, but I've maintained cooperation throughout, and exploiting others' trust purely for a few extra points in the last round feels inconsistent with the norm I've built. I'll stay with cooperation and be transparent about this tradeoff rather than defect.
